item.title: Consumers can’t get enough pistachio – but concerns about its environmental impact are growing
item.description: The crop has a large carbon footprint and is worryingly water-intensive.
item.content:encoded:
Pistachio production has more than trebled in the last 20 years. In 2024, more than 1.4 million tonnes were produced globally. Their popularity has only increased in the last two years, with a growing status as a trendy, luxury food item.

However, this rise in popularity has come with concerns around the pistachio’s environmental impacts. There are also questions around whether their production can withstand changing climate conditions.

Pistachios originated in modern-day Turkey and Iran. Despite being considered a nut, they are actually the seeds of pistachio trees. These trees thrive in a hot summer climate but require relatively cold winter temperatures to ensure the trees flower at the right time in spring. They also require dry conditions, as high humidity can reduce yields and leave the trees susceptible to fungal disease.

In the late 19th and early 20th century, pistachios were popularised in the US by migrants from the Middle East. By the 1930s, pistachio orchards were established in California. The warm, dry climate of California provided ideal conditions for pistachio trees, so much so that the US has now overtaken Iran and Turkey as the world’s largest producer of pistachios.

item.title: ‘The Anniversary’: This Italian novel examines a patriarchal nuclear family and its links to fascism
item.description: A post-traumatic memoir of survival in which the narrator calmly recalls the turbulence of the past.
item.content:encoded:
Andrea Bajani’s novel, the winner of the 2025 Strega Prize, is a radical exploration of the psychology of family estrangement. It appears at a cultural moment where therapy-oriented language such as “gaslighting”, “boundaries”, and “toxic” has percolated into the most intimate realms of daily life and adult children are fearlessly breaking taboos and going no-contact with their parents by denouncing the abuse within highly dysfunctional households. The Anniversary examines the social institution of the patriarchal nuclear family and its links to fascism in Italy, showing how domestic violence and coercive control by male members of the family are rendered invisible and normative.

The totalitarian infrastructures

In the novel, following a series of “unreliable memories”, the narrator recalls events that led to the final goodbye with his parents ten years ago. With the dysfunctional family at its centre, The Anniversary is an intensely psychological novel. Yet it does not treat the trauma of upbringing as a problem that can be solved through psychoanalysis. Instead, it moves outward to reflect on wider social conditions that allow totalitarian values to be reproduced in the private realms of the modern nuclear family.

item.title: Chirag Paswan files complaint against Hindutva influencer for ‘misusing’ his name
item.description: Swatantra Bharadwaj was arrested on Saturday in connection with the alleged assault of the father of a student activist during youth protests at Jantar Mantar.
item.content:encoded:
Union Minister Chirag Paswan on Friday filed a complaint against a Hindutva influencer for allegedly misusing his name in connection with the assault on the father of a student activist during youth protests at Jantar Mantar, ANI reported.

Paswan accused influencer Swatantra Bharadwaj of “falsely and publicly” citing his name, The Hindu reported.

A row had erupted after Bharadwaj claimed in a podcast that a call from Delhi minister Kapil Mishra helped him avoid arrest over the alleged assault, despite having “cracked the skull” of student activist Nishu Aazad’s father Sanjay Kumar.

In the same video Bharadwaj had said: “Chirag Paswan is my elder brother...I have everyone’s support.”

On Saturday, Bharadwaj was arrested and remanded to one-day police custody, The Indian Express reported.

On Friday, Paswan said that he and his party, Lok Janshakti Party (Ram Vilas), “stand firmly” with Kumar’s family. “Ensuring justice for them is a responsibility that both I and my party fully accept,” he was quoted as saying by ANI.

item.title: Has El Niño’s monsoon effect hit India’s kharif crops?
item.description: Former Union agriculture secretary Siraj Hussain says there is unlikely to be any significant loss of foodgrain production despite the rain deficit.
item.content:encoded:
The threat of a strong El Niño still looming, rainfall in this year’s monsoon season varied by the month. June was one of the driest in India’s history, closing at a 35% deficit whereas July was 1% above normal.

This “normal” rainfall in July was largely driven by Central India whereas East and South India had a large deficit. As of August 26, the all India seasonal rainfall stands at a 13% deficit, in keeping with the weather agency’s forecast of a below-normal monsoon. The deficit is still most pronounced in East and South India.

There have also been floods or flood-like situations in Assam, Himachal Pradesh, and parts of the National Capital Region, Uttar Pradesh etc. What does this mean for India’s primary cropping season, that is, Kharif? What does this mean for farmers, foodgrain production, food prices and ultimately, for consumers?

Reviewing preparedness for this Kharif crop season earlier in June, Union agriculture minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan had said, “There is no need to panic. What is required is preparedness and collective action.”

The Union government had urged states to promote short-duration crop varieties and those capable of delivering higher yields with lower water requirements. It further encouraged farmers to adopt crop diversification.

Parish Priest-in-Charge Father Samuel Hembrom of St Claret Church told the newspaper that the mob forced the body, which had already been lowered into the grave, to be taken out. The body was later taken to another cemetery in Bardhaman town, he said.

Hembrom said the mob had demanded to see the “papers for the burial ground”.

item.title: ‘Da’: A novel about a child’s observation of queer lives has its heart in the right place
item.description: Author Arathi Menon situates the novel’s political concerns in her 13-year-old protagonist’s own coming-of-age story.
item.content:encoded:
I held on tightly to the page when 13-year-old Ved is asked, “Do you think gay people should go to jail?” As though a child’s answer could change lives. In Arathi Menon’s novel Da, this question follows the reader with a sense of urgency. In 2013, as the courts debated the rights of queer Indians, the reader turns to the child in hope. Menon writes of those turbulent times, from the eyes of a young boy, with great vulnerability and hope.

At the outset, the novel is described as a politically charged story on laws around homosexuality in India and its resultant stigma. I went into it expecting great tragedy and suffering. However, two chapters in and I was surprised by the notoriously inquisitive voice of an adolescent boy being brought up by his dead mother’s brother.

Ved is bright and thinks a lot and thereby talks a lot. I was reminded of nine-year-old Mira from Bhavika Govil’s 2025 novel Hot Water; a stunningly written voice of a young girl watching her dysfunctional family. Mira would make good friends with Ved. item.title: Oxford University agrees to repatriate 39 Naga ancestral human remains taken during colonial rule
item.description: The Nagas have sought the return of the remains for years, with formal talks with Pitt Rivers Museum, which holds the varsity’s collection, beginning in 2020.
item.content:encoded:
The University of Oxford in the United Kingdom has agreed to repatriate 39 human remains belonging to the Naga people that were taken during colonial rule and put on display for decades.

The Pitt Rivers Museum, which holds collections from Oxford University, has the world’s largest Naga collection. It has around 8,000 Naga objects, including human remains, mainly skulls, and 178 objects that contain or may contain human hair. The museum removed all human remains from public display in 2020, Reuters reported.

Skulls and other body parts were often taken from Asia, Africa and elsewhere to Britain and other former colonial powers as “trophies”, and were traded, displayed or studied.

There are growing calls worldwide for such human remains, as well as stolen art and artefacts, to be returned to their communities as part of a wider movement seeking reparations for colonialism and slavery.

On Saturday, Naga Tribe Hobos and the Forum for Naga Reconciliation said in a statement that a Naga delegation will travel to the Pitt Rivers Museum to “claim and return” the ancestral remains.

The handover, scheduled for November, will be the largest repatriation of human remains from the museum, The New York Times quoted Pitt Rivers director Laura Van Broekhoven as saying.

item.title: 1,375 dead in Nepal-China flash flood, 275 Indians missing
item.description: Nearly 5,000 persons, including 618 foreigners, were missing in Nepal and more than 500 in China.
item.content:encoded:
The toll in the flash flood and mudslide in Nepal and China, which occurred on August 26, rose to 1,375 on Saturday. Of these, 1,344 deaths were reported in Nepal.

The remaining 31 deaths were on the Chinese side of the border, Chinese news agency Xinhua reported.

Nearly 5,000 persons, including 618 foreigners, were missing in Nepal and more than 500 in China. Those missing in Nepal included 275 Indians, the Ministry of External Affairs said on Friday.

External affairs ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said that 166 Indians have been rescued so far. He added that 1,907 Indian citizens had safely crossed into Nepal from China. There are no Indian travellers stranded on the Chinese side, he said.

Jaiswal also said that India had supplied about 95 tonnes of relief material to Nepal on seven aircrafts so far.

The floods occurred in the Rasuwa district along Nepal’s northern border with China. The mountainous district is located about 120 km north of Kathmandu. As there was no rainfall in the area, residents did not have a warning about the deluge.

The United States Geological Survey has said that the floods were caused by a glacial collapse that sent a wall of water and debris downstream, reported AFP.

item.title: September Indian nonfiction: Six new titles that revisit the past to question the present
item.description: A struggling mother’s journey from Bangladesh to India, a study of the effect of hate speech, the writings of Vijaya Lakshmi Pandit, and more.
item.content:encoded:
All information sourced from publishers.

It Started with Words: The Epidemic of Hate Speech in New India, Harsh Mander

Since 2014, hate speech in India has moved from the political fringe to the centre of public life. It is heard from election platforms and religious stages, repeated in television studios, circulated through WhatsApp and YouTube, and rewarded with votes, influence and profit. It calls for minorities to be boycotted, evicted, stripped of their livelihoods, driven from neighbourhoods and, increasingly, met with violence.

These words have consequences. They create the climate in which homes and shops are demolished, and ordinary citizens are lynched, intimidated, and made to prove, again and again, that they belong to their own country.

Human rights activist Harsh Mander examines how this hatred is produced, spread and protected; who profits from it; and what happens when those who incite fear also command the machinery of the state. Drawing on several case studies, including his own attempt to seek legal action against politicians for incendiary speeches delivered in the lead-up to the communal riots in Delhi in 2020, Mander asks whether the law can still protect the vulnerable – or whether it has become another weapon in the hands of the powerful.

item.title: United Nations adopts new map showing Africa larger
item.description: The United States was the only country to oppose the resolution to replace the 16th century Mercator projection that enlarged landmasses closer to the poles.
item.content:encoded:
The United Nations General Assembly on Friday adopted a new world map that makes the African continent appear larger and shrinks North America and Europe.

The nonbinding resolution piloted by Togo was aimed at adopting a more accurate representation of continental landmasses. While it was supported by 164 countries, including India, six countries abstained from voting. The United States was the only country to vote against the resolution.

The new map, known as the Equal Earth cartographic projection, improves the accuracy of the cartographic representation of the continents. Created by a group of cartographers in 2018, the new map makes Africa, Latin America, South Asia and Oceania appear much larger.

It replaces the 16th century Mercator projection, still the most widely used map in the world. It was devised by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator to solve a maritime navigation problem. Because straight lines on his map correspond to constant compass directions, sailors could use it to plot their courses, the United Nations noted.

However, while preserving directions, landmasses closer to the poles appear increasingly enlarged than those near the equator. For example, Greenland looks roughly the same size as Africa, even though the latter is about 14 times larger.

item.title: Manipur: More than 300 killed, 49 missing since 2023 violence
item.description: Chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh told the Assembly that 24,000 persons displaced amid the ethnic conflict remain in relief camps.
item.content:encoded:
At least 306 persons have been killed and 49 are missing in Manipur since the beginning of the ethnic violence in the state in May 2023, PTI quoted the government as having told the Assembly on Thursday.

State Home Minister Govindas Konthoujam provided the data recorded till August 31 in response to a question raised in the House. He said that the ethnic conflict had also caused widespread displacement and disrupted normal life across the state.

Ethnic clashes had first broken out in Manipur in May 2023 between the Meitei and the Kuki-Zo-Hmar communities.

The state was under President’s Rule between February 2025 and February 2026 after Bharatiya Janata Party leader N Biren Singh stepped down as the chief minister amid allegations from Kuki-Zomi-Hmar groups that his response to the violence had been partisan and that he had stoked majoritarianism.

Yumnam Khemchand Singh became the chief minister on February 4 this year.

He informed the Assembly on Thursday that 60,000 persons were displaced during the violence, which he described as an “unprecedented crisis”, The Telegraph reported. Of them, 36,000 internally displaced persons had been resettled and 24,000 remained in relief camps across Manipur.

item.title: Why is Goa allowing the 500-year-old Adil Shah Palace to crumble?
item.description: In the capital of Panjim, heritage buildings are being handed over to the casino industry and real-estate lobby for ‘beautification’ and ‘redevelopment’.
item.content:encoded:
At the rate priceless public heritage buildings are vanishing before our eyes in the Goan capital of Panjim (the Campal lighthouse is the latest infuriating example) or sinister plans seem afoot to hand them over to the casino industry or to the real-estate mafia for “beautification”, “redevelopment” or similar euphemisms for erasure, I felt it necessary to highlight our existing heritage and fervently hope we don’t ever have to mention them in the past tense.

It’s tragic how little we were taught in school about our heritage, and this problem of collective ignorance and apathy has gotten worse over time. It is this endemic ignorance that is partly responsible (apart from corruption and greed, of course) in illogical bureaucratic decisions adversely affecting Panjim’s heritage. What we know little or nothing about, we do not value. The writings of Percival Noronha, Vasco Pinho and Celsa Pinto are invaluable in addressing this lacuna.

The Old Secretariat is probably (after the Panjim church) our capital city’s most iconic landmark edifice, so it felt appropriate to begin with it.

item.title: In Odisha, drum-making traditions echo the rhythms of farm life
item.description: Families in a village in Bargarh district are keeping alive a craft shaped by soil, livestock, textiles, festivals and generations of knowledge.
item.content:encoded:
In Pahandi, a small village in Bijepur block of Odisha’s Bargarh district, the rhythm of a traditional baja or drum begins long before it reaches a festival ground. It begins with the earth.

Of the roughly 530 households in the village, most depend on agriculture, growing paddy, millets, green gram, ground nuts and other crops. But for eight households of the Chamar community, making traditional drums and other percussion instruments has supplemented their livelihoods for generations.

For Judhisthir Sagar, locally known as “Kutru”, the two occupations have always existed alongside each other. He inherited the craft of making baja from his ancestors, along with the practice of farming.

“Making drums and musical instruments is our identity,” said Sagar while tightening the strips of a newly made mrudanga, a two-headed percussion instrument widely used in traditional music. “We have been doing it for generations. It is our livelihood. We are proud to continue it.”

Apart from the mrudanga, other percussion instruments made in Pahandi include the godi mrudanga, udand khol, madol khol, dubi-tabla, pankuch, dhol and nisan. Each has a different shape and sound and a place in the cultural life of western Odisha.

item.title: Donations to six Gujarat-based parties exceeded those to national parties except BJP, reports BBC
item.description: The regional parties received Rs 1,700 crore during the fiscal year 2023-’24 as compared to Rs 1,480 crore of five national parties, including the Congress.
item.content:encoded:
Donations made to six political parties based in Gujarat were more than those made to national parties, except the Bharatiya Janata Party, in the financial year 2023-’24, BBC News Hindi reported on Friday.

The six parties categorised as registered unrecognised political parties were the Aam Janmat Party, Bharatiya National Janata Dal, Garib Kalyan Party, New India United Party, Satyawadi Rakshak Party and the Swatantrata Abhivyakti Party.

The six parties received donations of Rs 1,700 crore during the fiscal year 2023-’24, BBC reported citing data from the Election Commission and the Association for Democratic Reforms poll watchdog.

Five parties recognised as national parties at the time – the Congress, the Aam Aadmi Party, the Bahujan Samaj Party, the Communist Party of India (Marxist) and the National People’s Party – had received donations of Rs 1,480 crore.

The Aam Janmat Party had received Rs 620 crore in donations in the fiscal year, more than double of the Congress’ Rs 281 crore, BBC reported.

The financial year included the run-up to the 2024 Lok Sabha elections held in April and May that year.

While the five national parties had fielded 893 candidates in the 2024 general election, the six Gujarat-based parties had fielded 15 candidates.

item.title: Harsh Mander: Hindutva’s boycott calls seek the economic erasure of India’s Muslims
item.description: Through the Narendra Modi years, hateful calls have been amplified shrilly by affiliates of the Sangh, wrapped often in dangerous, even genocidal hate speech.
item.content:encoded:
The organised economic boycott of vulnerable and oppressed communities has scarred Indian society for millennia. India’s caste system excluded “untouchable” castes from employment in dignified vocations for since ancient times. This cruel arrangement has trapped them for centuries in want and penury, in illiteracy and in humiliating vocations.

The core of the Sangh project is to thrust Muslims into this same depressed zone.

Boycotts in history have also been a force for good. The boycott of foreign goods in colonial India led by Mahatma Gandhi shook the British Empire. When Rosa Parks in the United States in 1955 was found guilty of violating the Jim Crow racial segregation laws by refusing to vacate her seat in a bus for a white passenger, the Black community boycotted the bus system for 381 days. This brought the bus companies close to ruin, and the US Supreme Court judged the segregation laws to be unconstitutional.

However, the boycotts organised by the Sangh are part of their ambitious malevolent project of Hindu supremacism and anti-Muslim hate. Calls for economic boycott of Muslim businesses and workers dates back to the 1930s. item.title: ‘Laugh With Me’: Ruskin Bond offers poignant, humorous anecdotes about his writing career
item.description: Bond reminds the reader that ‘anger and resentment poison the soul’, so the ability to ‘laugh at yourself from time to time’ is the key to happiness.
item.content:encoded:
The writerly life can look like one never-ending party to readers who track their favourite authors on social media, hopping from book signings to literature festivals to award ceremonies. But this seductive illusion conceals the messy and uncomfortable realities that many authors have to live with. Ruskin Bond’s new book, Laugh With Me, is a joy to read because it sheds all pretence.

A first-person narrative by Bond, who celebrated his 92nd birthday in May of 2026, it grants privileged access to the inner world of a celebrated writer, and makes one chuckle along. He writes, for instance, of a time in his late twenties when he felt that his publishers were not doing enough to publicise a newly published short story collection, as a result of which it was not available in bookstores at Khan Market, Connaught Place, and Shankar Market in Delhi.

His frantic search led him to Janpath, where he found a copy at a small bookshop. “It was firmly wedged at the bottom of a pile of other writers’ bestsellers – Khushwant Singh, Shobha Dé, Harold Robbins, Vikram Seth, Roald Dahl – everyone on top of poor little RB,” he writes. In the draft voter list released on Monday, more than 47 lakh names were deleted. The names account for about 33% of the Union Territory’s electorate.

Of those removed, 43.3 lakh names, or 29.8% of the electorate, were marked as absent or permanently shifted. About 2.8 lakh persons were marked as dead and 1.4 lakh as excluded for having been enrolled at multiple places.

More than 20 lakh deletions in Delhi were in the 30 to 44 age group.

item.title: How Yikvot, a Kashmiri language preservation platform, hopes to help youth take to the language
item.description: An interview with Seerat Hafiz, who founded the platform in 2023.
item.content:encoded:
In 2023, Seerat Hafiz, who studied conflict studies and psychology in college and university, founded Yikvot, which means “together” in Kashmiri, to preserve the Kashmiri language and culture, and to connect and engage with her mother tongue at a time discourses around Kashmiri literature were hard to find for young people like herself.

It began with hosting interactive reading sessions of important works of Kashmiri literature with academics and writers like Shafi Shouq and Neerja Mattoo. The most ambitious effort of the platform was to recover the vast, overlooked corpus of translation both into and out of Kashmiri. For instance, Russian greats like Leo Tolstoy and Fyodor Dostoevsky have been translated into Kashmiri, and this revelation reframed for Hafiz how far translation has shaped Kashmir’s literary history.

Today, Yikvot is devoted to literature, arts, and culture – it is a space where Kashmir’s artists and writers can publish their own work. The next step is to develop an app, which many users find easier to navigate and more travel-friendly. The app will feature, among other things, “Rasm-e-Khat”, the Kashmiri keyboard, “Alif Bey”, a space to learn to read, write, and speak Kashmiri, and “Kutub Kha’na’e”, a library of Kashmiri literature. item.title: Maafi, Kafi, Anchahi: The unwanted daughters in Haryana’s voter rolls
item.description: The SIR exercise was an unsettling reminder that disparaging names for women were common until a few decades ago.
item.content:encoded:
The names of some women voters stood out while I was looking up my parents’ details in the 2002 voter list for the Special Intensive Revision exercise being conducted in Haryana.

“Bhateri” and “Bharpai” seemed to be common names that were repeated across voter lists. Bhateri comes from the Haryanvi word “bhatera”, which means enough, while the word “Bharpai” indicates something that is surplus or plentiful.

It was an unsettling realisation that these names for women were common up until a few decades ago.

They are a reflection of Haryana’s deep-seated preference for sons. The 1981 Census noted that Haryana had only 870 females per 1,000 males, far below the national average of 933 females per 1,000 males. Voters born around 1981 would have been at least 21 years old when the SIR was conducted in 2002.

Conversations with women in my family and neighbourhood revealed that these names were quite common in Haryana till some decades ago. For the women bearing such names, it was humiliating but also something they had come to live with.

item.title: In Texas, politicians are treating everyday Muslim practices as a threat
item.description: Some claim that Islam doesn’t really count as a religion and that it is actually a political ideology bent on ‘world domination’.
item.content:encoded:
Elected officials across Texas are increasingly treating ordinary Muslim religious practice – prayer, dress, marriage counseling, even mosques themselves – as evidence of a political threat and saying so openly.

“I won’t rest until every Muslim is gone,” Bo French, the Republican nominee for Texas railroad commissioner, wrote on social media in June. Since late 2025, Texas officials have investigated plans for a Muslim-friendly housing development outside Dallas, as well as a small Dallas organisation that offers religious divorce counseling. Governor Greg Abbott also designated the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the country’s largest Muslim civil rights group, a foreign terrorist organisation under Texas law.

item.title: A new book examines why some Indians turned to ‘terrorism’ early in the struggle for independence
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Colonialism, Tradition and Reform: An Analysis of Gandhi’s Political Discourse’, by Bhikhu Parekh.
item.content:encoded:
Though India’s struggle for independence was largely non-violent, it was constantly shadowed and vitalised by a relatively small but vocal and, at times, highly effective terrorist movement. The movement began in the 1870s as a reaction against the way in which the colonial government set about responding to the political trauma of 1857.

As we saw elsewhere, most Indians thought that the government in London was sympathetic to their aspirations, but that its good intentions were systematically frustrated by its narrow-minded representatives in India. Queen Victoria’s proclamation seemed to them to indict previous Indian governments and to promise better times. The Raj’s subsequent failure to satisfy the legitimate expectations it had itself aroused led to bitter disappointment. To reach the village, Matla, one has to trek a kilometre up a hill, on muddy trails and slippery slopes.

item.title: How the US war has changed power equations in Iran
item.description: The fight is no longer about whether to bargain but the precise ways and means of improving Iran’s position before it commits to anything irreversible.

When Washington unveiled its economic “D-Day” on August 19, the latest tightening of the financial siege and the blockade around Iran’s ports, it believed it was applying decisive leverage. But in Tehran the move was read as something else entirely – as confirmation that the US still prefers pressure to any settlement it might one day have to honour.

Across a political system that agrees on almost nothing, the interpretation was remarkably uniform. The economic stabilisers around the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, saw the US as reneging on a deal, while Ahmad Vahidi’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) commanders saw their own warnings about American perfidy vindicated.

So whatever faith remained in Iran about US willingness to close a deal has thinned further. That erosion of trust now shapes what Tehran will and will not accept.

A decade after the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act was passed, its vision of empowering people with disabilities and removing barriers to accessing justice is unfulfilled.

This failure is most evident in the functioning of the Office of the Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities and its state counterparts, even though they were strengthened as part of the 2016 law to ensure substantive rights and meaningful access to justice for disabled persons.

The 2016 act envisaged a government-wide effort, requiring ministries, departments and public institutions to review and align their laws, policies, procedures and practices with its mandate.

item.title: How a ‘super El Niño’ could make India’s monsoon drier – yet more dangerous
item.description: It could create an apparently contradictory situation: less rain over the season as a whole, but heavier rain when it does rain.
item.content:encoded:
India is currently in the middle of its summer monsoon, but this year’s rainfall presents an interesting paradox. Much of the country has received less rain than usual so far, yet has still been hit by severe floods and landslides. In Kerala, for example, devastating floods occurred despite the overall monsoon rainfall remaining well below average.

A weaker monsoon does not necessarily mean an absence of extreme rainfall. Rainfall can be highly uneven, with long dry spells broken by intense cloudbursts that cause flooding and landslides. This year’s experience in Kerala illustrates the apparent contradiction: a season that is dry overall can still produce devastating rainfall.

Amid this highly uneven monsoon, attention is also turning to something happening thousands of kilometres away in the tropical Pacific Ocean: El Niño.

It is well established that El Niño years, when certain parts of the Pacific are warmer than usual, are often associated with weaker Indian monsoon rainfall. Meanwhile La Niña – the opposite state to El Niño – tends to favour wetter conditions. This year, El Niño conditions have developed rapidly in the Pacific, with forecasts suggesting it could become exceptionally strong.

The Supreme Court on Tuesday asked the Union government to submit its views on introducing a totaliser system to count votes recorded in a cluster of electronic voting machines, reported Live Law.

At present, votes cast in elections are counted booth-wise. A totaliser would allow votes recorded in multiple machines to be counted together. This can make it difficult to determine how any particular booth voted.

item.title: More Indian students are abandoning higher education as degrees no longer seem worth the cost
item.description: Political control over educational institutes has lowered the value of academic degrees, which no longer seem worth the cost and time.
item.content:encoded:
While the youth protests were underway at the Jantar Mantar in the first week of July, the Central government published two crucial reports on higher education enrollment: the All India Survey on Higher Education for 2022-’23 and 2023-’24.

The findings were alarming. For the first time since 2011, there has been a decline in the number of Indian students pursuing undergraduate degrees. In 2023-’24, undergraduate enrolment decreased by 93,321 students compared with the previous academic year, representing a decline of 0.29%. This decline at national level might look small. But for a developing country like India enrollments for higher education are supposed to grow fast.

Maharashtra was among the states with the sharpest declines: 5% of Class 12 students here did not enroll in the undergraduate enrollment. This means that nearly 200,000 fewer young people in the state opted for degree programmes compared to the previous year. The number dropped from 35,04,046 in 2023-’24 from 36,88,956 in 2022-’23.

item.title: Mankind destroyed whatever was gifted as life: Tagore’s lament for the environment 87 years ago
item.description: The Nobel Laureate initiated a tree planting festival at Sriniketan on September 2, 1938 when he gave a prescient address, translated into English here.
item.content:encoded:
About a century ago, long before environmental degradation became the crisis of our times, Nobel Laureate Rabindranath Tagore had sounded early warning bells about the destruction of forests.

Though Tagore was born in the city of Kolkata, he had a deep and abiding contact with nature from childhood, and it shaped his many-sided genius in diverse ways. As an adolescent, he accompanied his father Debendranath to the foothills of the Himalayas, an experience he wrote about in his autobiographical notes.

Later, he was a frequent visitor to a zamindari estate in Shilaidaha, now in Bangladesh, where many of his short stories and songs were written while on a boat on the mighty river Padma. He had experienced the vast expanse of nature – in the sky, in the mountains, in the rivers and the flat, verdant lands of the Bengal delta.

Simultaneously he witnessed the urbanisation of the sleepy villages around Kolkata and Kolkata itself, and lamented the oppressive bounds of concrete and the lessening of contact between human beings and nature. item.title: ‘Maxxing’ is just self-care and improvement repackaged for social media
item.description: Constantly focusing on how to maximise ourselves may inadvertently cause us to become more focused on what is wrong with us.
item.content:encoded:
If you want to improve yourself, your health or your lifestyle, you need to do it to the “maxx” – according to social media, at least.

If you want to better your appearance, you need to try “looksmaxxing”. If you want to fix your diet and look after your gut, you should be “fibremaxxing”. And if you want to improve your social skills and be more charming, you really ought to be “personality-maxxing”.

But all of this maxxing might not actually be a good way to motivate yourself into healthier habits. In fact, it may have the opposite effect – and may even cause stress.

The language of “maxxing” has roots in the gaming concept of “min-maxing”, in which players strategically maximise desirable attributes while minimising less useful ones to create the most effective in-game character. The concept then made it’s way to the mainstream, most notably through “looksmaxxing”: making focused, and sometimes extreme, efforts to maximise physical attractiveness.

The suffix has since been adapted in multiple health and wellbeing spaces. If there is an aspect of life that could be improved, it can probably be maxxed.

item.title: How a male Marathi theatre star defined the role of the perfect Hindu wife in the 20th century
item.description: Bal Gandharva’s star persona became a site where respectable Hindu femininity was produced and commodified.
item.content:encoded:
For much of the 20th century, the most admired wife in Marathi-speaking India was not a woman at all.

Bal Gandharva (1888–1967), a celebrated impersonator of Marathi sangeet natak (musical theatre), played devoted heroines with such conviction that film actresses well into the 1970s were trained to reproduce his mannerisms.

How did a man come to define middle-class femininity with such authority?

My recently published research traces Gandharva’s enactment of womanhood from the stage to the marketplace.

It reveals how his star persona became a site where respectable Hindu femininity was produced and commodified – a project that the theatre industry, emerging consumer culture and Hindu nationalist politics each exploited for their own ends.

Staging respectability

India’s pervasive caste system divides Hindus into distinct groups based on which caste they are born into, with certain castes regarded as “higher” than others.

Some of these “lower” castes are made up of hereditary performers: families with a lineage of performing arts. Historically, women from these communities were allowed – and sometimes expected – to perform and entertain.

But Marathi sangeet natak, which emerged in the mid-19th century, was a predominantly upper-caste and middle-class practice.
